Who we build for

Five operators, five different problems

We are a services business, and services only work when they are shaped to the operation buying them. A tribal property with a four-person IT team does not want what a Macau VIP floor wants, and neither of them wants what a route operator running nine rulebooks wants. Here is what we bring to each.

USA · commercial

Casinos

Single properties and multi-property groups running IGT, Aristocrat or Light & Wonder underneath. We build around the casino management system you already have rather than asking you to replace it.

USA · sovereign

Tribal casinos

Asia · integrated resorts

Asian casinos

Engagement models

Five ways to put this team on your problem

Services are the larger part of what we do, and the shape matters as much as the skills. A tribal property replacing a booth application does not want the same contract as a slot manufacturer who needs a squad to hold a product for three years. Pick the shape, then we scope the work.

Ongoing

Dedicated gaming squad

A named team that stays on your product between releases, with a product owner, engineers, QA and a release manager. They keep the floor knowledge instead of handing it back at the end of a statement of work.

  • Monthly, with a notice period rather than a cliff
  • Scales up for a certification window and back down after
  • Common for solutions companies and multi-property groups

Fixed scope

Build to a date

A defined system, a fixed scope and a date that usually belongs to a regulator or a property opening rather than to us. Discovery first, then a plan we hold ourselves to, with the lab submission planned from week one.

  • Kiosks, booth applications, portals, integrations, reporting
  • Certification evidence packaged as the build proceeds
  • Handover includes the runbook, not just the repository

Assurance

Certification and QA support

Someone else built it and now it has to pass. We take the product through GLI or BMM submission, build the regression suite that survives more than one release, and fix what the lab sends back.

  • Test planning, automation and defect cycles
  • GLI and BMM submissions with evidence assembled as we go
  • Works on code we did not write

Managed

Run it for us

Application support, monitored infrastructure, release discipline and an SLA-backed hotline. For operators whose internal IT team is three people and a pager, this is usually the engagement that comes first.

  • 24x7 cover with a named escalation path that does not change
  • Monitoring and patching, with release windows around your floor
  • Sustaining engineering on systems we did or did not build

AI and agents

Bring a process and we build the agent that runs it, against the applications you already have. Six weeks from queue to unattended, with shadow running in the middle so your team agrees with it before it submits anything.

What we have built

Two decades of it, one layer at a time

We did not arrive at the gaming stack from the top. We built a loyalty engine, then the kiosk that fed it, then the POS integration that made the points mean something at the restaurant till, then the reporting that proved any of it worked, then the compliance layer the regulator asked for. Twenty years of that.

The result is a team that has already shipped every layer below, on live floors, for casino operators, slot manufacturers and lottery organizations. Most vendors own one of these layers and hand you an integration problem between the rest. That is the gap this list exists to close.

Casino management systems

Multi-property CMS work with a single player card across the enterprise: player management, floor search, VIP host tooling and rewards. Delivered as new builds, as replatforms, and as enhancements to systems that were already carrying production traffic on a working floor.

Player loyalty and engagement

Loyalty marketing engines with tiers, points, comps and balances, plus promotions, giveaways, sweepstakes, raffle and lottery management. One card and one balance across every property and outlet, so a point earned at a machine spends at the restaurant.

Table, floor and mobile

Table game data, trend displays and pit tooling, alongside mobile player management for VIP hosts — player search on the floor, profile and tier updates, rewards issued where the player is standing rather than back at the club booth.

Self-service kiosks

Player marketing kiosks for sign-up, lost card replacement, tier point printing, offer redemption and win or loss statements — integrated to the CMS platforms already on the floor, with anti-money-laundering controls built in because an unattended terminal moves value.

The integrations that were the real work

CMS integrations across IGT, Aristocrat and Light & Wonder, including Scientific Gaming CMP. G2S at the machine and S2S between platforms, alongside OpenAPI, MSMQ and TIBCO. Micros, Infogenesis, Agilysys and OpenTable at the point of sale; Opera and Alice on the hotel side. Built to survive the next upgrade cycle.

Data, BI and reporting

Slot revenue per square foot, player average daily theoretical, campaign performance and operational KPIs. Custom report builders for the questions that were not on anyone’s original list, and dashboards people actually open on a Monday.

Compliance and risk

Title 31 reporting and anti-money-laundering detection down to the kiosk, including slot-floor scenarios for structured cash-in and cash-in with no play. Identity and age verification by ID scan, self-exclusion checks, fake ID detection and audit trails throughout.

AI and ML operations

The newest layer, and the one built on all the others: personalization, next-action recommendation, churn and value forecasting and fraud detection — with the data pipelines, model deployment and monitoring underneath, rather than a model in a notebook.

See eight of these builds in detail

AI on the floor

Intelligence where the decision happens

AI earns its place in a casino when it shortens the distance between a signal and an action. These are the four places we see it pay for itself.

Offers at the moment of churn

Most offers arrive after the player has left the property. A rule engine that reads play as it happens can predict the walk and place the right offer before it happens, redeemable on the spot.

Redemption without leaving the seat

A tap at the table redeems a valid offer in seconds. No walk to the booth, no promo chip handling, and almost nothing asked of the dealer.

Advantage play, caught early

Behavior models watch table play for counting patterns and collusion, raise real-time alerts and leave an auditable record for the surveillance team.

Value you can forecast

Player value, tier movement and offer liability projected forward instead of reported backward, so marketing spends against what is coming.

Agentic automation

The work nobody should still be typing

Two systems that were never integrated, and a team of people re-typing between them. We solve it with an agent that drives the existing application the way a person does: it finds the screen, moves through the tabs and fills the fields. No vendor API, no change to the system underneath, and nothing near the wager flow.

Player enrollment

Player enrollment, entered by an agent

Enrollment backlogs are where this bites hardest. Paper sign-up cards from a promotion, an event sheet, a bus manifest, a list from a partner, or a player file from a property you have just acquired. All of it has to end up in the casino management system, and most of the time that means a person typing it in one tab at a time. The agent works through the same enrollment screens your staff use, so the CMS does not have to change and no import route has to exist.

Before

Enrollment cards stacked in a tray. Someone keys each one into the CMS across five tabs, days after the player was standing in front of you, with duplicates found later.

→
After

The batch is read overnight, checked for duplicates and age, entered into the CMS, and the card number written back. Only the exceptions reach a person.

Step 01

Ingest. A scanned enrollment card, an event sign-up sheet, a group manifest or a player file from another property lands in a watched folder.

Step 02

Read. Fields are extracted and normalized: name, date of birth, address, contact preferences, identification, source of the sign-up.

Step 03

Check. Duplicate search against the existing player base, age and identification validation, and self-exclusion screening before anything is created.

Step 04

Enter. The agent opens the enrollment screen, moves through each tab, fills every field, applies the club and tier defaults and submits.

Step 05

Reconcile. The card number is written back to the source record, and anything ambiguous goes to a human queue instead of being guessed.

Where else it lands

Same agent, other screens

Jackpot and hand pay entry

Slot floor paperwork re-keyed into the back office system, with the tax and threshold fields filled consistently and an audit trail behind each entry.

Terminal reports into accounting

Daily meter and revenue reports read, normalized and entered into the accounting and compliance systems instead of being reformatted by hand each period.

Offer and comp loading

Campaign lists and comp allocations entered against the right players, so marketing stops waiting on a queue to get an offer live.

License and permit renewals

Renewal records maintained across jurisdictions, with expiry dates tracked and filings prepared from what is already recorded.

Machine moves and asset changes

Floor moves reconciled between the floor system and the asset register, so the two stop disagreeing about where a machine is.

Vendor invoice matching

Invoices matched to service tickets and purchase records, with anything that does not reconcile routed to a person rather than paid.

Every action the agent takes is logged as a person would be logged, so the work stays auditable. Nothing here touches the wager flow, the random number generator or anything inside the certified boundary. This capability is also packaged as a product: see Agent360 →

Assurance

The lab is not a surprise at the end

Gaming software gets judged twice: once by your users and once by an independent lab. We plan for both from the start, and we support GLI and BMM submissions rather than handing you a build and wishing you luck.

A dedicated QA function runs alongside engineering — requirement analysis, test planning, case creation and execution, defect cycles, then final check and UAT — across unit, integration and system levels.

  • Functional testing — interface, database, batch, usability and user acceptance
  • Non-functional testing — performance and stress, security, recovery
  • Mobile and network testing — plus game adaptation across devices and estates
  • Test automation — regression suites that survive a release cycle rather than one
  • Certification support — GLI and BMM lab submissions, evidence packaged as we go
  • 24x7 hotline — SLA-backed support, because a floor does not keep office hours

Protocols and platforms

We build to the standards the floor already speaks

A gaming product that cannot hold a conversation with the systems already on the floor is a rewrite waiting to happen. Protocol work is not something we bolt on at integration time — it shapes the data model on day one.

G2S

Game to System, for machine-level communication: meters, events, jackpots, device state and remote configuration. We design to it rather than translating into it afterwards, so a new machine type is a configuration change and not a project.

S2S

System to System, for the exchange between platforms: player, account and promotional data moving between CMS, loyalty, marketing and third-party systems. We have built open player data exchange over S2S alongside OpenAPI, MSMQ and TIBCO.

ICCP and SmartCasino

Control-tier certified on Walker Digital Table Systems' Intelligent Casino Control Platform — the first solutions provider certified under the program — with access to the full control API set for the table floor.

CMS integration experience

The three platforms most casino floors actually run on. We have integrated to all of them — from kiosks and loyalty engines to player data exchange and reporting.

IGT

Player marketing kiosk and loyalty integrations against IGT casino management, including sign-up, card reprint and tier point flows on the floor.

Aristocrat

Kiosk and player management integrations to Aristocrat CMS, with enrollment, profile and rewards handled without a trip back to the club booth.

Light & Wonder

Integrations across the Light & Wonder estate, including Scientific Gaming CMP, and automated meter and revenue ingestion for route operations.

The integration problem

One player. One record. Every touchpoint.

When the loyalty system, the floor, the restaurant and the host booth each hold their own version of a player, marketing guesses and finance reconciles. Integration is not a technical nicety here. It is the difference between knowing a guest and guessing at one.

We work to the exchange standards the industry already runs on, so your systems keep talking after the next upgrade cycle, not just on go-live day.

How we get there

Idea to floor, without the eighteen-month wait

Our innovation model exists to shorten the gap between a good idea and something patrons can actually touch. Each stage has a real exit, so you always know what you are approving next.

Stage 01

Rapid prototyping

A working prototype in weeks, not a slide about one. Validates the idea, keeps iteration cheap and gives your stakeholders something concrete to react to.

Stage 02

Market testing

Put it in front of real users and real floor conditions. This is where assumptions break cheaply and where we learn what the patron actually does.

Stage 03

Stakeholder alignment

Operations, marketing, compliance and IT agree on scope, roles and the definition of done before build hardens. Fewer surprises at UAT.

Stage 04

Commercialization

Certification support, scalable infrastructure, staged rollout and a go-to-market plan that accounts for staff training and floor disruption.

Stage 05

Growth at scale

Additional properties, jurisdictions and outlets on the same foundation, with performance held steady as volume grows.

RouteHub · the platform for slot route operators

Request a walkthrough Why now

Who it is for

The operations it was built around, and why it fits

The mechanics of cash, service and compliance are the same whether the machines sit in a tribal casino, a bar route or a single small floor. What changes is the reporting line, who signs, and which part of the platform earns its keep first.

01 / Tribal casinos

Tribal gaming operations

Single or multi-site · tribal commission reporting

Sovereign gaming runs to its own compact and its own gaming commission, not a state revenue office. Reporting has to satisfy the tribal commission and the terms of the compact, and the estate often spans a main floor plus satellite and off-reservation venues under different rules.

  • Reporting templated to the tribal gaming commission, not a state format
  • Compact revenue-share calculation and audit trail held per property
  • Main floor, satellite and off-reservation venues in one estate view
  • Per-property access control so each site sees only its own numbers
  • Cash custody evidence in the format a compact audit asks for

02 / Route operators

Mid to large distributed gaming routes

500 to 5,000 machines · multi-state capable

This is the estate the platform was designed around. At this scale the operator is running a fleet, not a floor: hundreds of venues, a depot, collectors on the road and a compliance calendar per state. Fills judged by feel start costing real money.

  • Predictive cassette fills and load optimization across the whole route
  • Territory-aware routing, depot to stop to bank, with signed hand-offs
  • Venue revenue share, contracts and license expiry tracked per location
  • Service dispatch triaged by severity and routed to the nearest technician
  • Jurisdiction-templated filings for every state the route touches

03 / Smaller operators

Smaller gaming operators and single-market routes

Under 500 machines · single market

Below a few hundred machines the problem is not fleet complexity, it is that one or two people are doing everything by hand and there is no budget for an enterprise rollout. The platform starts as the module that hurts most and grows from there.

  • Start on one module, on one route, with your existing report feeds
  • Cash custody and collection history without a back-office team
  • Venue owner portal so performance questions stop coming by phone
  • Filings produced from the work already recorded, not rebuilt each period
  • Add modules as the estate grows, on your own timeline

04 / Casino floors

Casino slot floors and cash operations

Single property · floor and cage

A casino floor is a route with the travel removed. The vault, the cassettes, the kiosks and the service queue behave the same way, and the same visibility over cash on street, drops and stranded credits applies inside one building.

  • Vault, kiosk and machine custody inside a single property
  • Cash on street, drops and stranded credits by machine and bank
  • Service tickets triaged and tracked against machine history
  • Cashless and voucher mix reported alongside cash
  • Title 31 and AML evidence produced as a by-product of the work

The market

A national footprint, run under a different rulebook in every state

Gaming outside a casino floor — video gaming terminals, video lottery and restricted-location slots — is licensed state by state, with no federal framework over any of it. Eight states run it as a route business, and the operators inside those markets have outgrown the tooling they started with. Growth no longer comes from adding venues at home. It comes from crossing state lines, and every line crossed adds another regulator, another reporting format and another tax treatment to carry.

~130,000Regulated route and distributed-gaming machines in service across the eight state markets
8 statesIllinois, Nevada, Montana, Louisiana, Oregon, South Dakota, West Virginia, and Pennsylvania at truck stops only
~48,000Terminals in Illinois alone, across roughly 8,500 licensed locations: the largest distributed market in the country
No federal frameworkLicensing, reporting cadence, tax treatment and renewal cycles differ in every jurisdiction

Illinois sets the scale

Close to half the country’s regulated terminals sit in one state, spread across thousands of small licensed locations rather than a handful of large ones. Per-location terminal limits were raised from five to six in 2019, with higher allowances at truck stops.

Growth is coming from consolidation

Legislative expansion into new states has largely stalled, so the estates are growing by acquisition instead. An estate assembled that way arrives as several incompatible back offices at once, which is usually the moment a platform decision gets made.

Adjacent markets, different statutes

Georgia’s redemption-only amusement machines and Nebraska’s regulated skill games sit outside the eight, but they are run by the same operators with the same field economics: collections, service calls and per-location reporting.

The skill-game question

Bringing unregulated skill games under license is under active debate in several states. Wherever it happens, an installed base that exists today becomes a licensed, reportable estate with filings attached, and it needs a back office from day one.

Machine and location counts are approximate, drawn from state gaming board and state lottery reporting, and move with each reporting period.

Why RouteHub exists

Route operations outgrew the spreadsheet years ago

Distributed gaming operators now run hundreds of venues, thousands of terminals and a fleet of collector vans on tooling that was never designed for any of it. The cost shows up as blind dispatch, late fills, unexplained variance and players nobody can name. RouteHub replaces that stack with one system every role signs into.

Player development, powered by AI

The next action, not a catalog to guess from

A host with sixty players in their book is making dozens of small judgment calls a shift: who to call, what to offer, how much, and when. Host360 does not take that call away. It puts a recommendation and its reasoning next to the player, so the judgment starts from the pattern across every player rather than from memory.

  • A specific action, with a number attached. The offer, the amount and the night — scored on modeled uplift against offer cost, not on tier alone.
  • Reasons the host can read. Every recommendation shows what drove it: visit gap against the player's own pattern, what they redeemed last time, what they ignored.
  • Confidence shown honestly. A thin bar means the model is guessing, and the host is told so rather than being handed false precision.
  • Override is one tap and it is recorded. When the host knows something the model does not, their decision becomes training data instead of an argument.
  • Churn signals arrive early. The player drifting away surfaces at nineteen days, not when someone runs a quarterly report.
  • Liability tracked continuously. Marketing sees what is outstanding against redemption as it happens, not at month end.

The model is trained on your own play, redemption and visitation data, inside your environment. It recommends; it never issues an offer on its own, and every suggestion, acceptance and override carries an audit trail.

Where AI fits

A better instinct, not a replacement for one

Hosts already know their players. What they do not have is the pattern across ten thousand of them. That is the only job we give the model.

The app suggests the offer most likely to land for this player, at this tier, on this night, instead of leaving the host to guess from a catalog.

Why it exists

The offer usually arrives after the player has left the seat

Electronic table games sit awkwardly between slots and live tables. The play is seated and sustained like a table, but the player is often uncarded, and anything promotional has to be issued by hand. Tap wagering removes both problems at the terminal.

On most ETG floors today

  • Play is anonymous unless the player volunteers a card at the podium
  • An offer is issued at the booth, so it lands after the session, not during it
  • Promotional instruments are handed out, counted and reconciled by staff
  • Rated ETG play depends on someone at the podium recording it
  • Marketing finds out what worked at month end, from a report

With NFC Tap Wagering

  • A tap identifies the player at the terminal in under a second

How a tap works

Five steps, and none of them involve the podium

From the player’s point of view it is one gesture. Underneath, it is an identity resolution, an eligibility check and a committed transaction inside the certified boundary.

01

The player taps

A phone or a contactless player card is presented at the reader on the terminal. No app to open at the table, no card to hand over, no queue at the kiosk.

02

The player is identified

The tap resolves to a player account and a seat, so the session is attributed to the right person from the first hand rather than reconstructed afterwards.

03

The wager or the offer is validated

Eligibility, limits and offer terms are checked against the loyalty and promotions rules before anything is committed. An invalid offer never reaches the game.

04

The control platform commits it

The digital wager or the redemption is committed through the certified control integration on the ETG, inside the boundary the regulator already recognizes.

05

The record is written

Player, terminal, amount, offer and outcome are written once and available to marketing, finance and audit from the same record.

What it does

Six things it changes on the ETG floor

Tap to wager

A digital wager placed from the player’s phone or card at the terminal position, running through the certified control integration rather than around it.

In-session redemption

A valid offer redeemed in seconds while the player is still in the seat, so it lands at the moment it can still change the session.

Nothing asked of the floor staff

No promo instrument to issue by hand, no manual reconciliation at the podium, and no change to how the game itself is dealt on screen.

Rated play, captured

The tap identifies the player at the terminal, so ETG play is attributed to the right account without anyone recording it by hand.

Auditable by design

Every wager and every redemption carries a record with player, terminal, time and outcome — which is what makes a marketing mechanic defensible.

Inside the certified boundary

Built on the control APIs our WDTS certification opens, so digital wagering is supported through the program rather than bolted alongside it.

Inside the certified boundary

Built on the control APIs, not beside them

In September 2025 Walker Digital Table Systems named Droisys the first certified solutions provider in its SmartCasino Certified Solutions Program. Tap wagering is built on what that certification opens.

Control tier, not read-only

Gaming/Products/Agent360

Agent360 · AI agents for gaming operations

The work nobody should still be typing

Every casino and every route has a queue of work that exists only because two systems were never introduced to each other. Agent360 puts an AI agent on that queue. It drives the applications you already run, through the same screens your staff use, so there is no vendor API to buy, no change to the system underneath and nothing anywhere near the certified boundary.

It ships as a product: a runtime, a console, a library of gaming agents ready to configure, and an exception queue for the cases a person should still see. Where your process is your own, we build the agent for it and hand it over running.

See the agent library Book a working session

Who it is for

The teams it was built around, and why it fits

Agent360 is bought by whoever owns a backlog that grows faster than the headcount allowed to clear it. That is a different department in every operation, so the product is licensed per agent rather than per seat, and each agent is scoped to one job.

01 / Casino operations

Player operations and marketing

Enrollment, offers and comps

The backlog that costs the most is the one between a player signing up and that player existing in the casino management system. Promotion cards, event sheets, bus manifests and files from an acquired property all end up in the same tray, and the offer that should have followed lands a fortnight late.

  • Enrollment entered from scanned cards, sheets and manifests overnight
  • Duplicate, age and self-exclusion screening before anything is created
  • Campaign lists and comp allocations loaded against the right players
  • Card numbers written back to the source record, not retyped
  • Only the ambiguous cases reach a person

02 / Finance

Accounting and back office

Daily reports, matching, close

Meter and revenue reports arrive in one format and are needed in another, so somebody reformats them by hand every period. Invoices arrive against service tickets nobody has time to match. None of it is hard. All of it is slow, and every hand-off is a place a number changes.

  • Terminal and meter reports read, normalized and entered
  • Vendor invoices matched to service tickets and purchase records
  • Jackpot and hand pay entries keyed with tax and threshold fields consistent
  • Anything that does not reconcile routed to a person rather than posted
  • A close that starts from entered data instead of a chase

03 / Compliance

Compliance and licensing

Filings, renewals, evidence

Multi-jurisdiction operators carry a renewal calendar that nobody owns full time until something expires. The information needed is already recorded somewhere. The work is assembling it into the format each regulator wants, on the date each regulator wants it.

  • License and permit records maintained across jurisdictions
  • Expiry dates tracked and filings prepared from what is already recorded
  • Evidence packs assembled in the format the regulator asks for
  • Every agent action logged with the same identity trail as a person
  • Read-only mode where a regulator requires a human submit

04 / Route operators

Distributed gaming back offices

Venue paperwork, multi-state

A route back office is nine rulebooks and several hundred venues held together by spreadsheets and email. The people doing it are good at it, which is exactly why they should not be spending the morning re-keying a meter report into an accounting system.

  • Manufacturer reports ingested and entered without reformatting
  • Venue contracts, licenses and revenue-share records kept current
  • Machine moves reconciled between the floor system and the asset register
  • Filings assembled per jurisdiction from recorded work
  • Runs alongside RouteHub, or alongside whatever you already use

05 / Solutions companies

Gaming solutions companies

OEM and white label

Slot manufacturers, systems vendors and lottery suppliers carry the same back-office drag as their customers, plus a support queue of their own. Agent360 is available under your brand, deployed into your environment, with the agents built against your own applications.

  • White-label deployment under your name and your support contract
  • Agents built against your product, not only against third-party systems

What you license

A product, not a proof of concept

Most agent work stalls at the demo because the demo was the easy ninety per cent. What makes this a product is the unglamorous ten: what happens when the screen has moved, when the record is ambiguous, when the regulator asks who did that, and when someone needs to know what it saved this month.

The agent runtime

Drives desktop and browser applications the way a person does: it finds the screen, moves through the tabs, fills the fields and submits. No vendor API, no database writes, no change to the system underneath. When a screen moves, the agent adapts rather than failing silently.

Document and queue intake

Watched folders, mailboxes and shared drives. Scanned cards, event sheets, manifests, meter reports and vendor files are read, extracted and normalized before anything is entered, with the original kept alongside the record it produced.

Checks before entry

Duplicate search, age and identification validation, self-exclusion screening and threshold rules run before a record is created, not after. A batch that fails a check does not get half entered.

The exception queue

The agent is measured on what it refuses as much as on what it completes. Anything ambiguous goes to a person with the source document, the reason it stopped and the fields it was unsure of. Nothing is guessed to keep a completion rate looking good.

The console

What ran, what it entered, what it escalated, how long it took and what it cost. Volume and hours returned per agent per month, so the renewal conversation is a number rather than a feeling.

Audit and access

Each agent runs under its own named service identity with its own permissions, scoped to the screens it needs. Every field entry and every submit is timestamped and retained, so the trail an auditor follows looks the same as it would for a person.

Deployed on your infrastructure or in your private cloud. Player data does not leave your environment, and no gaming data is used to train a shared model.

Each one is configured against your systems rather than built from scratch, which is the difference between a fortnight and a quarter. Start with one, on one queue, and add the next when the first has paid for itself.

Getting live

One queue, six weeks, a number at the end

We do not start with a platform rollout. We start with the single queue that is costing you the most, run the agent beside your team until it agrees with them, and only then let it run unattended.

Week 1

Pick the queue. We watch the work being done, count what it costs today and write down what a correct outcome looks like.

Week 2

Configure the agent against your systems, in a test environment, with your own documents rather than samples.

Weeks 3-4

Shadow mode. The agent proposes, your team confirms, and every disagreement tunes it. Nothing is submitted yet.

Week 5

Supervised live. The agent enters, a person reviews the batch, and the exception queue gets its thresholds set properly.

Week 6

Unattended, with exceptions still going to a person. The console reports volume, hours returned and accuracy from day one.

Your own process, not one from the library? That is the same six weeks. Bring the queue and the screens, and we build the agent against them and hand it over running, under the same license and the same console.

The boundary

Where an agent is not allowed to go

This is a regulated floor, and the fastest way to lose a gaming license is to let something clever run somewhere it was never approved to run. The limits below are product limits, not policy we ask you to trust us on.

Agent360 works in the same places your back-office staff work: the administrative screens, the reports, the records. It stays out of everything that a lab has certified.

  • Nothing touches the wager flow — no play, no outcome, no bet, no settlement
  • Nothing touches the random number generator or anything inside the certified boundary
  • No direct database writes — the agent uses the same screens and the same validation your staff do
  • Named identity per agent, with permissions scoped to the screens that agent needs and nothing more
  • Full audit trail on every field, every submit and every escalation, retained to your policy
  • Human in the loop by default — unattended running is a decision you make per agent, not a default we ship
  • Your data stays yours — on your infrastructure, and never used to train a shared model

Business challenge

Advantage play is caught late or not at all.

Advantage play is caught late or not at all. Transformation

  • An auditable record of every alert, the evidence behind it and the action taken
  • Delivered as a secure web service, so it reaches surveillance, the pit and management without a desktop rollout

Outcomes

What it changed for the business

  • Surveillance covers more tables without adding headcount
  • Investigations start from a recorded evidence trail, not recollection
  • Nothing touches the wager flow or the certified boundary, so the floor keeps running

Across a group, a patron needed a different card for every property, and updating an address at one meant it was wrong at the others.

Transformation

What we built

  • Self-service by kiosk, mobile app and web portal against the same account
  • Card reprints, offer and comp redemption, and profile updates without staff
  • Real-time balances, tier progress and status
  • Sweepstakes activation and printing
  • One card earning and redeeming across participating properties and outlets
  • A profile update at one property reflected at the others
  • Built for both enterprise groups and single-site operations

Outcomes

What it changed for the business

  • Routine booth traffic moves to self-service, cutting queue and overhead
  • The program keeps working at peak, when staff are least available
  • Cross-property earning and redemption raises the value of membership
  • One patron record replaces several, so marketing works from truth
  • Personalized offers become possible because behavior is unified
  • Single-site properties get enterprise capability without enterprise cost

Self-service kiosksOne cardCross-propertyEnterpriseLoyalty
